Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un

North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.

This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.

Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.

"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack

Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far

But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.

The country has consistently denied such claims.

Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.

The company's spokesperson said that a net $4.72bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday.

The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.

That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.

"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.

The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.

Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.

The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

'I've always looked in bins for clothes'

Darryl Baker was shocked to see piles of clothes dumped beside the recycling bins outside her local supermarket.

On several trips to the dumpsters she has also found a host of other items, such as "a perfectly decent" Ikea picture frame and children's scooters.

Always on the lookout for ways to save money and appalled by the waste, the thrifty mother-of-two from north London asked supermarket staff if she could take some of it.

Permission granted, "I got my children entire new wardrobes," says Darryl, 39, adding that she's stuff put away for years to come.

During a six-month stint this year, "I have probably saved hundreds of pounds," says the freelance journalist.

Darryl reels off the names of brands she has salvaged - Ralph Lauren, Nike and The North Face, among others. "My mind was blown," she says. "This stuff is just strewn all over the floor."

Darryl Baker takes the clothes for herself and her children, and to sell

In addition to finding clothing for her children and her nephews and nieces, she keeps some for herself. Others she donates or sells, including recently getting £30 for a men's Barbour jacket.

Darryl has joined the ranks of so-called dumpster divers – people who rummage through commercial bins for treasures. Motivations include saving money, giving items to charity and disgust at how often perfectly usable items are being consigned to waste - or a combination of all three.

Texan Jeff Ferrell has been rooting around in trash for more than 50 years.

"I still dumpster dive every day by bicycle," says the 72-year old, who lives in Fort Worth, and has written books on the topic. "I still enjoy it as much, or more, than ever."

Jeff considers himself a "bit of Robin Hood mixed with anarchist direct action", only scrounging in more affluent neighbourhoods and giving away many of his finds.

"Almost everything in our home is scrounged, and I never buy, for example, soap or toiletries or medical supplies, or shoes and clothes and tools and garden supplies," he says.

Jeff Ferrell sells some of what he finds, and gives away other items

Jeff looks for discarded metal to sell at a scrapyard which, he says, earns him around $150 (£110) every two weeks. His wife sells his other finds, such as "an antique or piece of jewellery", on eBay.

Through savings and selling the more valuable items, he estimates his finds are worth "tens of thousands of dollars a year".

While dumpster diving may have been considered taboo in the past, it's now something many people are proud to do and post about online.

Millie Diamond, a London-based stylist, posts videos on Instagram of her rummaging through bins. But she has a very specific aim - to unearth fabrics and clothing that she can salvage and refashion into new items, some of which she then sells.

Millie Diamond turns dumped textiles and clothes into new outfits

She estimates that one dress she found was worth £600.

"I'm a bit of a magpie. I like collecting things off the street or anywhere that there's a freebie. If I see something that catches my eye, then I'll grab it."

Millie, 36, began bin diving after spotting some fabrics discarded by a business that had shut down. "I literally clambered into the bin. It turned out it was loads of vintage clothes."

For Charlotte Bayford in Essex it's all about timing. Her best finds come when students at Essex University head home for the summer and ditch anything they don't want to take with them.

This includes half-filled toiletries. "I haven't bought shampoo for eight years," says the 44-year-old sales assistant. "I'd say that has saved me some money."

Like other dumpster divers, Charlotte gives a lot of her finds to charity. But she has also filled her house with salvaged objects, and sells on some valuable items.

Food, as long as it remains sealed, is fair game too. "I've found tins of Heinz baked beans, perfectly fine. I'm quite happy to eat those," Charlotte says.

Charlotte Bayford gives some of her finds to charity

But is taking things out of bins and keeping them acceptable in the eyes of the law?

Jeff, who is professor emeritus of sociology at Texas Christian University, says many US cities have made the practice illegal, including New York, Cleveland and Wichita.

"Dumpster diving is considered illegal [in such places] because that which is thrown away now belongs to the city... or to the private company that provided trash services," he explains. Any dumpster diver also risks trespass charges.

In Fort Worth, where Jeff lives, items can only be removed from bins if they are on public land , external .

In the UK, Sunjay Versani of Duncan Lewis Solicitors says it depends on the circumstances.

"In many cases involving genuinely discarded goods, prosecution is unlikely," he says.

"But there is no general rule that something is free to take simply because it has been put in a skip or bin. If in doubt, the safest approach is to ask the owner or business for permission."

Forever chemicals - or PFAS - can enter the human body after leaking into soil and waterways

The government is launching its first study into the levels of so-called 'forever chemicals' in the UK population.

By taking blood and urine samples, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) hopes to gain a better understanding of any potential health risks caused by the substances also known as PFAS, as well as other potential contaminants like lead and arsenic.

It said current evidence suggested the possible health impacts associated with PFAS are likely to be limited, but said the strongest links found in large population groups have been to raised cholesterol and lower birth weights.

The first results are expected next year.

PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have been used prolifically since the 1940s and 1950s because they are resistant to water, oil and heat.

It is why they have been placed in thousands of items such as pots and pans, clothing and foams used to fight fires.

But because they do not break down easily in the environment - hence the name 'forever chemicals' - they have raised health concerns in recent years.

Two are already banned in the UK - PFOA and PFOS - because prolonged exposure to them can increase the risk of cancer, according to the World Health Organization. , external

But the study of PFAS is an emerging field with more than 15,000 types to research.

The UKHSA will take blood and urine samples collected through the existing Health Survey for England , external to establish baseline levels of PFAS, lead, arsenic, bisphenols, phthalates and flame retardants in the population.

Inside Health: What we do and don't know about PFAS

In an exclusive interview with BBC Radio 4's Inside Health, Dr Edward Wynne-Evans, director of radiation, chemicals, climate and environmental hazards at the UKHSA, said there are gaps around "what different levels of exposure mean for an individual's long-term health".

There are growing concerns among people living near sites where there has been contamination from the two known toxic PFAS, and they have chosen to get individual blood tests.

In September, blood tests found "really high levels" of one of the cancer-causing forever chemicals (PFOA) in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory.

But the UK government does not recommend individuals get routine PFAS blood testing because there is no "established clinical intervention" if they have elevated levels, Wynne-Evans said.

"If you are going to do a test where you cannot recommend an action to follow, we would not normally recommend a test."

He said that this study would help "build an evidence base to better understand what might be happening".

Speaking before this study was announced, Prof Tony Fletcher from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said he believed there is a low level of PFAS in everyone's blood.

"If we tested a random sample of anybody's blood, we would measure [PFAS] in low levels."

"We are not all dying because of this but at higher levels [and in larger populations] they have been associated with adverse health effects."

For the two banned PFAS - PFOA and PFOS - the known risks , external include increased cholesterol, an increased risk of cancer, reduced antibody levels following childhood vaccinations and a range of endocrine effects linked to the thyroid and lower birth weights.

"I have met with people living in an area with contamination - they are angry," Fletcher said.

"What I try and explain to them is we have found these causal associations between exposure and effect in studying large populations. Although at an individual level, the chances of you getting some bad disease or some adverse health effect is quite low."

He stated the important thing is to stop ongoing exposure, to avoid any long-term effects.

Inside Health was produced by Imogen Harper and Tom Bonnett. And additional reporting by Esme Stallard.

Four planned "hyperscale" data centres are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs

The UK government's ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 could be undermined by its new deal on AI data centres, according to BBC research.

During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said data centres would be allowed to build onsite power generation while they wait for a grid connection.

BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four planned "hyperscale" data centres - including three in the south of England - are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs, creating more CO2 than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.

Labour MP Toby Perkins, who chairs the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said a substantial increase in the use of natural gas "can't be the future".

"Government absolutely shouldn't be in the business of just saying anyone who wants to bring it here, can do whatever you like to power it, because that is not acceptable," he said.

Toby Perkins MP, chair of the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said the use of gas power for AI data centres was "not acceptable"

The government said data centres were "essential to Britain's economy" and that its new Data Centre Covenant set clear expectations for developers to pay a fair share of the costs they impose on the energy system and deliver benefits for local communities.

Data centres are warehouses full of powerful computer servers used to run a vast range of digital services, including streaming, banking and public services and have been part of the British landscape for more than two decades.

But a new generation of data centres due to come on stream in the next few years will operate on a much larger scale to cope with the growing computing demand needed for increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence technology.

They will consume considerably more energy than their predecessors at a time when the National Grid is already struggling to meet demand.

Ofgem, the energy market regulator, says data centre developers are seeking connections totalling 72 gigawatts. The peak electricity demand across the whole country last year was 45 gigawatts.

There are plans to construct an AI data centre on the the site surrounding Redcar's former blast furnace

Such is the demand for access to the already under-strain national electricity grid, some data centre developers have been told they could be waiting up to 10 years for the system to be upgraded to provide them with a connection.

Nathan MacWhinnie, head of market intelligence and oversight at Ofgem, said: "In a lot of places, the grid is at capacity. I think sometimes it's easy to forget the scale of the demand of these connections. These projects are sometimes the size of cities."

In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a British Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for priority grid connections.

But he also said that where grid connections were unavailable, developers would be permitted to generate their own power on-site.

BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four data centres are already looking at using gas-fired power stations to meet their electricity needs.

If continuously running at full capacity, our calculations show they would require 1.3 gigawatts of power and could produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year. This could be more than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.

Oliver Hayes, of environmental charity Global Action Plan, is concerned about the use of gas-fired power to supply data centres with electricity

Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at environmental charity Global Action Plan, said: "If we're powering by gas that means local communities are going to have huge gas turbines on their doorstep, and they are going to be generating a huge amount of local air pollution and a huge amount of noise and they will be using a huge amount of water from the local water supply."

The developments already considering on-site gas vary in scale.

At Acre Slough, west of London, developers say they could use gas engines with a generating capacity of up to 49.5 megawatts while waiting for a National Grid connection, something they expect could take at least 10 years.

At Wapsey's Wood, next to the M40 in Buckinghamshire, a proposed 200-megawatt gas power station could operate until sufficient grid capacity becomes available, currently not expected until 2040.

"It would be a disaster for us environmentally," said Buckinghamshire independent councillor Ed Gemmell, who also leads the Climate Party.

"If allowed, it sets a precedent that we could be getting gas-fired power stations all over the country and that would make it extremely difficult for us to hit any of our environmental and net zero targets."

Is it time to press pause on AI data centres?

An increasing number of large AI data centres are waiting in the UK energy supply queue - but will meeting that demand derail the road to net zero?

Quest Park has proposed building a data centre on the site of a quarry pit next to the planned Universal theme park in Bedfordshire. It would have a power load - the total amount of electrical power drawn at any given time - of 1 gigawatt, the equivalent to 200,000–250,000 average UK homes.

David Kohler, director of Quest Park, has previously told the BBC the company's energy mix was still a "work in progress" and that incorporating renewable power was "sensible" but had to be "feasible".

He said creating 1 gigawatt of solar electricity would require an area equivalent to 15% of Bedfordshire, and that wind power was "intermittent and expensive".

He said the company was considering alternative technologies that did not rely on gas combustion.

In Cardiff, a data centre developer is also seeking permission to build a temporary energy centre that has turbines with a maximum generating capacity of 49.9 megawatts.

Planning documents say it could operate for up to five years if the site cannot secure an electricity grid connection quickly enough. Developer Curtis Hall has described the turbine plan as a "worst-case scenario".

Quest Park wants to build a data centre on the site of a quarry pit

All four projects say they intend to connect to the national grid when it can meet their electricity needs, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels.

The government said its priority was connecting data centres to the grid so they could benefit from the UK's rapidly decarbonising power sector.

It said any behind-the-meter power generation would be tightly controlled, time-limited and allowed only for exceptionally strategic projects where sufficient capacity could not be secured by other means.

A government spokesperson added: "Data centres are essential to Britain's economy, supporting everything from online banking to NHS services.

"Pausing development would send jobs, investment and data overseas and leave us more reliant on other countries for critical digital infrastructure. That's why we're backing their growth while making sure it's done responsibly.

"Our new Data Centre Covenant sets clear expectations for developers to minimise water use, pay their fair share of energy costs and deliver benefits for local communities."

Beth Jenkins' cancer was initially missed after told she was "too young" to have the disease

A woman who said she was told by a GP she may be experiencing "medical anxiety" after finding a lump in her breast was later diagnosed with cancer.

Beth Jenkins, 42, visited a locum GP at her practice with concerns that a lump on her right breast had grown significantly. But she said she was told she was "too young to have breast cancer" and it may be linked to postnatal depression instead.

However, it was lobular breast cancer , external , with a 5cm (2in) tumour and the disease had spread to three lymph nodes.

Practice 1 Keir Hardie Health Park said it could not discuss individual cases but encouraged patients to "make a second appointment" if they had concerns about their health or care.

The mum-of-two from Merthyr Tydfil first noticed a "small pea-sized" lump in her breast in 2018, but, after an ultrasound, she was told it was likely glandular tissue and no biopsy was carried out.

A few years later she had given birth to her daughter Robyn and, while changing her nappy, Robyn accidentally kicked the right side of her chest.

It was then that Jenkins noticed the lump had become "massive", so she visited her GP practice in October 2024.

She said, being 40 at the time, she was told she was "too young" to have breast cancer and the lump might be linked to an infection or "medical anxiety" as she had postnatal depression, and was prescribed antibiotics.

She said: "I haven't got medical anxiety, otherwise I'd be up the hospital and doctors' every week."

Beth said she "instantly thought of my children" after her diagnosis

Two weeks later she returned to the practice while taking her baby for an appointment and decided to speak to a female GP about her concerns.

The GP reviewed her notes and advised her to submit an e-consult, saying she should have been referred straight away.

"So I went straight home, did what she said and the same locum doctor picked it up and he rang me," she said.

"He was like, 'you're still a bit anxious about this lump here.' I said, 'I'm not anxious. I said it's something, it's non-infection. I need to have it seen to'."

Beth lost her hair, but decided to shave it off first to be able to "control" what she could while being treated for breast cancer

She was referred to a breast clinic and diagnosed on 14 November 2024. The cancer had spread to three lymph nodes by the time it was found.

"Me and my dad, we just sat in shock really. I didn't even cry, I didn't get upset," she said.

Despite the devastating news, Jenkins, a police officer, praised the specialist team, saying the consultant reassured her: "I promise you I will get rid of this."

At first, Jenkins had a mastectomy and initially told her eight-year-old daughter Fallon that she had a "boob job".

She laughed: "Her remark to me was, 'why did you just have the one boob done and not the other one?'"

Jenkins decided to tell Fallon she had cancer before starting chemotherapy and radiotherapy - which caused her to lose her hair.

She had further preventative treatment, but experienced serious complications including neutropenic sepsis , external .

"They said if I had gone there [to the hospital] 24 hours later, I wouldn't have survived," she said.

Beth decided to tell her daughter Fallon about her cancer diagnosis before she started chemotherapy

Jenkins is classed as having no evidence of disease but will be monitored for 15 years.

She said people have described her as "one of the lucky ones" but added: "Lucky would be not to have cancer at all, and not for my kids to see what they've had to see for the last two years."

Jenkins described GPs as "the gateway to the services" and stressed "if you can't get past the GP to get to that service, there's people dying".

In the UK, routine NHS breast screening is not automatically offered to 40-year-olds, as standard invitations begin at 50.

Dr Lee Campbell from Cancer Research Wales said, although uncommon, there were about 100-115 cases of breast cancer in women under 40 each year in Wales.

"Age should not be a deciding factor for referral for further investigations if symptoms present in younger women," he added.

Dr Lee Campbell says there is "an inequity" on how GPs apply referral guidelines for people aged 40 and under

Jenkins hopes sharing her story will encourage others to "keep pushing" for answers and to fight to be heard.

"If I hadn't had a voice, or if I'd just listened to that doctor, I could be sitting here now and they'd say, 'it's in your bones, in your brain'," she said.

"So many more people are sat in the house right now who should have been diagnosed and by the time they go back they're terminal.

"Cancer didn't care that I was a mother to a 10-month-old... cancer doesn't discriminate".

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines state that people 40 and under should be referred for further investigation if they have an unexplained breast or armpit lump, with or without pain, or skin changes that could indicate breast cancer.

Research by Cancer Research Wales found "an inequity" on how GPs apply these - some follow them closely while others rely on experience or instinct.

Campbell said: "We are currently working with researchers and primary care centres across Wales to ensure guidelines are followed and best practice is pursued.

"With respect to cancer, this will enable GP practices to go from gatekeepers to case-finders and will ensure cases like Beth's are dealt with sooner and not readily dismissed."

Beth Jenkins has decided to create Breast Fest, a charity event on 14 November to raise money for Merthyr Cancer Aid

Since raising concerns publicly, Jenkins said her GP practice had been "pretty forthcoming" and put out a statement on social media in July 2025.

It said a "serious diagnosis was unfortunately missed at first.

"Thankfully, she returned to see another member of our team who sent an urgent referral - but had they not, the outcome could have been very different. In the patient's own words 'trust your instincts'."

Jenkins said she had "tried to turn a negative into a positive."

To mark two years since her diagnosis, she decided to create Breast Fest, a charity event to raise money for Merthyr Cancer Aid on 14 November that has raised £6,000 from ticket sales alone.

"People are being so kind. It's gone really well and I'm hoping to raise a lot of money," she said.

The Shetland Isles previously had many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles

Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.

Recent analysis by the Daily Telegraph , external also revealed that there have been more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables linking Britain with Europe and the US.

These cables carry the majority of telecoms data abroad.

The growing importance of undersea infrastructure prompted a parliamentary report , external last year to warn of security vulnerabilities in areas including transport and supply chains, financial services and payment systems.

There are also concerns that the £30m SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland could be a Russian target.

But do the Shetland Isles really need better protection by the military?

A Russian vessel was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia

In recent years there have been a number of incidents in the Baltic Sea where underwater cables have been damaged or completely cut.

In December last year, Finnish police detained a vessel sailing from Russia, which was suspected of damaging an undersea telecoms cable running from Helsinki to Estonia, across the Gulf of Finland.

In 2022, Shetland was cut off from the mainland after a nearby subsea cable was damaged .

And last year there were two cable breaks in Shetland , which disrupted internet services and, in one case, took weeks to repair.

There has been no suggestion that there was any Russian involvement in the Shetland incidents but they demonstrate how fragile the cables are and show the devastating effect on the islanders when they are damaged.

In July, Royal Navy warships and helicopters spent 21 days monitoring Russian activity in UK waters and the North Atlantic - this was a 25% increase on previous time spent monitoring.

The recent Telegraph revelation of more than 500 incidents where Russian boats have been stationed above undersea cables has also caused concern.

History teacher and tour guide Jon Sandison said military presence in Shetland reduced in the second half of the 20th Century

Jon Sandison, a high school history teacher and Shetland tour guide, said there were real concerns that Shetland could be attacked after Germany invaded Norway in 1940, during World War Two.

"Shetland could have been a stepping stone towards Orkney and mainland Scotland," he said.

There were many army, naval and RAF personnel stationed across the isles and coastal defences were built to defend Lerwick and the rest of the archipelago.

The SaxaVord Spaceport sits on a former RAF base and RAF Skaw played an important role in efforts to detect enemy aircraft from 1941.

RAF Saxa Vord was later involved in Nato's radar network to monitor Soviet activity during the Cold War.

Scotcast: Is Shetland really in Putin’s sights?

The radar station closed in 2006 but it was revived in 2018 for Arctic surveillance as an automated remote radar head.

Sandison said that while military presence reduced in the second half of the 20th Century, Shetland's geographical position would never change.

"Where we are in the UK is always going to be a pivotal geographical location in relation to the North Sea, the Arctic Circle and wider scope of Britain," he said.

He added that coastal infrastructure was built very quickly during the Second World War.

"Air raid shelters, anti-aircraft defences - it's remarkable how much was built in a short space of time," he added.

"Not much of the infrastructure remains. It's part of our history, and part of our past."

MP Alistair Carmichael has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure

First Minister John Swinney has accused the UK government of leaving "Scotland's vast coastline dangerously exposed".

He pointed to waters off Shetland as an area of significant Russian activity.

"I don't think we've got nearly the presence in those areas that we require today," he told BBC Scotland News .

Liberal Democrat MP Alistair Carmichael, whose constituency covers Shetland, has urged the UK government to step up efforts to protect critical infrastructure.

He told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme: "This is something we do need to be taking seriously.

"We're not expecting an imminent problem here but this is a time where the government is already telling us that we should all be keeping baked beans and a wind-up torch in a cupboard."

UK plans emergency powers to protect undersea cables

I do not have confidence UK is safe from Russian threats - Swinney

Damaged cable cuts Shetland off from mainland

Carmichael added that if the world had changed so much, some of the decisions made by the UK government to remove military presence from the northern isles may now need to be looked at again.

He said that over the last 20 years, there had been just one local full-time soldier running a reserved unit in Shetland but they were now managed from the Scottish mainland.

Carmichael said there should be restoration of a full-time presence to support the unit and more reserves should be recruited in the northern isles as numbers were low.

But he added: "If the signal that the government is sending the community is that we don't even think its important enough to send one full-time solider to run these units then you can't expect the community themselves to be particularly enthusiastic about it."

SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport

SaxaVord in Unst is the UK's first fully-licensed spaceport with several companies interested in using the site to launch small satellites into orbit.

In September, the UK government announced investment of £30m in the project, as part of a new £7.8bn space strategy.

Alistair Carmichael said the spaceport would draw more attention to Shetland as a significant asset.

The German and UK governments plan to use SaxaVord to deepen their co-operation on space .

In October, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor Friedrich Merz met in Berlin and announced plans to work more closely on economic growth, defence and technology.

SaxaVord Spaceport was identified as a focus for immediate work on European launches.

Two German companies are currently in a race to be the first to test a rocket in Shetland.

Chief executive Scott Hammond said: "The space strategy is absolutely critical.

"We're at the heart of the UK government's plans for assured access to space.

"That's also for our economic and Nato partners."

He added that the UK government had joined as one of its majority investors, with a member on the board, but stressed that SaxaVord Spaceport was still a private commercial company.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We are clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses.

"Through the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force, we are leading allied activity across the High North, strengthening Nato's northern flank and increasing our ability to respond rapidly to emerging threats.

"This government is also investing in the capabilities needed to meet those threats, with £1.5bn backing Atlantic Bastion to deliver a next-generation Hybrid Navy and a further £330m to strengthen the protection of critical undersea infrastructure."

The zeptoverse explained by BBC science correspondent Pallab Ghosh

Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.

A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

Many sub-atomic particles are created by smashing the insides of atoms together

Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

Dr Harry Cliff is one of a team of British scientists involved in the research

The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.

"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.

But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.

It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope .

Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.

"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.

"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."

Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper is questioning whether to continue her physics research career in the UK or find work abroad

Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.

"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.

She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.

The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.

UK research hit by cuts despite record science funding

Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".

But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.

"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.

The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI , CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set , so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai .

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file ( how ). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space , where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json . Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment : the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic .

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md .

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model :

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space .

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study , the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Perezida w'Amerika Donald Trump yamenyesheje inteko ishingamategeko y'icyo gihugu ko ashaka gukura u Rwanda n'Afurika y'Epfo muri gahunda yo ku byorohereza mu bucuruzi bikorana n'icyo gihugu, guhera ku itariki ya mbere Mutarama (1) mu mwaka wa 2027.

Ayo masezerano yitwa AGOA (African Growth and Opportunity Act) atuma ibihugu bibyemerewe byo muri Afurika byohereza muri Amerika ibicuruzwa bibarirwa mu bihumbi nta mahoro (misoro) bitanze.

U Rwanda ruri muri AGOA kuva mu mwaka wa 2000, ari na bwo iyo gahunda yatangiye.

Jamieson Greer, uhagarariye ubucuruzi Amerika ikorana n'amahanga, yasohoye itangazo ku wa mbere avuga ko isuzuma ngarukamwaka ryasanze ibyo bihugu byombi bikora ibikorwa bidahuye n'ibisabwa kugira ngo igihugu cyemererwe kuba muri iyo gahunda.

Yongeyeho ko ubutegetsi bwa Trump bwanamenyesheje ibyo bihugu bibiri icyo cyemezo.

Mu mwaka wa 2018, kuri manda ya mbere ya Trump, Amerika yari yakuye ibicuruzwa by'imyambaro by'u Rwanda muri gahunda ya AGOA , nyuma yuko ruzamuye cyane amahoro rwaka ku myenda n'inkweto byambawe biva mu mahanga bizwi cyane ku izina rya caguwa. Imwe muri iyo myenda n'inkweto biva muri Amerika.

Ubutegetsi bwa Trump bwavuze ko icyo cyemezo cyo gukura ibyo bihugu muri AGOA cyafashwe kubera inzitizi ku bucuruzi n'ishoramari ry'Amerika, hamwe n'impungenge ku nyungu zayo zo mu rwego rw'umutekano w'igihugu n'ububanyi n'amahanga muri ako karere.

Ku Rwanda, Washington yanagaragaje impungenge ku burenganzira bwa muntu, kuri politike y'amashyaka menshi, ku butegetsi bwubahiriza amategeko no ku burenganzira bw'abakozi.

Amerika ifashe iki cyemezo mu gihe hashize hafi icyumweru minisiteri y'imari y'Amerika ifatiye ibihano minisiteri y'ingabo z'u Rwanda na banki ya Zigama CSS, igenewe abasirikare n'abandi bakora mu nzego z'umutekano n'ubutasi, kubera uruhare bashinjwa rwo gufasha umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa M23 mu burasirazuba bwa Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo (DRC).

U Rwanda ruhakana gufasha izo nyeshyamba, rukavuga ko rwashyizeho "ingamba z'ubwirinzi".

Minisiteri y'imari y'Amerika yavuze ko minisiteri y'ingabo z'u Rwanda yategetse abasirikare babarirwa mu bihumbi kurwana ku ruhande rw'inyeshyamba za M23 mu burasirazuba bwa DRC, igatanga intwaro, ibikoresho n'imyitozo.

Nta cyo leta y'u Rwanda yahise itangaza kuri iki cyemezo gishya cy'Amerika. BBC Gahuzamiryango yandikiye leta y'u Rwanda iyisaba kugira icyo ibivugaho.

Mu cyumweru gishize, ubwo yavugaga kuri ibyo bihano Amerika yafatiye u Rwanda, umuvugizi wa leta y'u Rwanda Yolande Makolo yasohoye itangazo avuga ko "U Rwanda rwiteguye gushyira mu bikorwa Amasezerano ya Washington, igihe cyose leta ya Kongo [DRC] izagaragaza ubushake bwo kubahiriza inshingano zayo, kandi umuhuza akita ku buryo impande zose zabazwa inshingano ku byo ziyemeje".

Amerika ivuga ko ibyo bihano bigamije gushimangira amasezerano ya Washington Perezida w'u Rwanda Paul Kagame na Perezida wa DRC Félix Tshisekedi basinye mu Kuboza (12) mu 2025, ku buhuza bw'Amerika. Ayo masezerano agamije kurangiza iyo ntambara no kwagura ubucuruzi n'ishoramari mu karere, ariko imirwano yarakomeje.

Mu byo asaba, harimo ko DRC irandura (cyangwa kubuza gukora – "neutralisation") umutwe w'inyeshyamba wa FDLR ufitanye isano n'abashinjwa kuba barakoze jenoside yabaye mu Rwanda mu mwaka wa 1994. U Rwanda ruvuga ko uwo mutwe uteje inkeke ku mutekano warwo ndetse ruvuga ko kuba uwo mutwe uba mu burasirazuba bwa DRC ari yo mpamvu rufata "ingamba z'ubwirinzi".

U Rwanda na rwo rusabwa gukura ingabo zarwo ku butaka bwa DRC no kureka gufasha umutwe wa M23, mu kwezi gushize wahindutse FRN, uyobowe n'uwahoze ari Perezida wa DRC Joseph Kabila, ukaba ushaka gukuraho ubutegetsi bwa DRC.

Kuri Afurika y'Epfo, Amerika yanavuze kuri ruswa.

Greer yagize ati: "Ubutegetsi bwa Trump burimo gukora mu gutuma abafatanyabikorwa bacu bo muri Afurika bafata ingamba za ngombwa zo kuzuza ibisabwa kugira ngo bemererwe [kuba muri AGOA]."

Minisitiri w'ubucuruzi n'inganda w'Afurika y'Epfo Parks Tau yavuze ko icyo cyemezo cy'Amerika "kibabaje", avuga ko Washington irimo kugaragaza ibibazo bishya bitari byaragaragajwe mu biganiro ku bucuruzi hagati y'ibihugu byombi byatangiye mu mwaka wa 2025.

Tau yagize ati: "Tuzakomeza kwihutisha kohereza ibicuruzwa by'Afurika y'Epfo mu masoko atandukanye mu rwego rwo kurinda imirimo."

Ambasaderi w'Amerika muri Afurika y'Epfo Leo Brent Bozell III yavuze ko bibabaje kuba gahunda z'Afurika y'Epfo zaratumye ikurwa muri AGOA.

Yanditse ku rubuga nkoranyambaga rwa X ati: "Ibi [bibaye] byari byitezwe kandi byashoboraga kwirindwa bivuye ku kuba leta y'Afurika y'Epfo yaranze impungenge za nyazo z'Amerika."

Amerika isohoye iryo tangazo mu gihe hari umubano urimo ibibazo hagati ya Washington n'ibyo bihugu byombi, uko kubikura muri AGOA guteganyijwe kukaba guteje inkeke ku mubano n'Amerika mu by'ubucuruzi bubyorohereza.

Mu mwaka ushize, Perezida Trump yashinje Afurika y'Epfo kuba irimo gukorera jenoside abazungu b'Abanyafurika y'Epfo, ubwo yari ari kumwe mu nama na Perezida w'Afurika y'Epfo Cyril Ramaphosa mu biro bya White House, ikirego Afurika y'Epfo ihakana. Amerika yanatangije gahunda yo guha ubuhunzi abazungu bo muri Afurika y'Epfo bo mu bwoko bw'Aba-Afrikaners.

Uganda yataye muri yompi uwahoze ari icegera c'umukuru w'igisirikare akaba yabaye n'umuhanuzi (umujanama) wa Perezida, Peter Elwelu, inyuma y'uko yiketswe kugira uruhara mu bikorwa bigamije guhungabanya umutekano w'igihugu.

Umuvugizi w'imfatakibanza w'igisirikare ca Uganda, Chris Magezi, yavuze ko Elwelu, adondora nk'"uwagararije", yafashwe ku mugoroba wo ku wa mbere, kandi ko azogezwa muri sentare kugira imumenyeshe ibirego.

Ifatwa ryiwe rije inyuma y'imisi mike umukuru w'igisirikare ca Uganda, Jenerale Muhoozi Kainerugaba, atangaje ko yakoroye Lieutenant General Elwelu amapete, akamugira umusirikare wo ku rwego rwo hasi.

Peter Elwelu ntaco aravuga ku vyo yagirizwa.

Elwelu yamenyekanye cane mu mwaka wa 2016, igihe yahagararira ibikorwa vy'igisirikare vyahitanye abantu benshi, vyabereye ku kirimba c'umwami w'akarere yagirizwa - ico gihe - kurongora umurwi washaka kwiyonkora ku gihugu. Inyuma y'aho, yaciye agirwa umukuru w'igisirikare.

Mu nyuma, yaraduze mu mabanga gushika aho agirwa icegera c'umukuru w'igisirikare, imbere y'uko agenwa kuba umuhanuzi wa Perezida.

Muri Rusama (5) 2024, Reta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika zamufatiye ibihano ku vyaha bijanye n'ihonyangwa ry'agateka ka zina muntu, harimwo ubwicanyi ndengerabutungane. Yakukurutse muri Myandagaro (8) 2025.

Ku wa mbere, umuvugizi w'igisirikare yavuze ko inzego z'umutekano zafatiye muri imwe mu nzu za Elwelu inkoho 15, impuzu z'igisirikare hamwe n'imodoka zibiri zo mu bwoko bwa pick-up.

Magezi, afatiye kuri kamwe mu burere bwo mu buseruko bwa Uganda, yavuze ati: "Elwelu amaze igihe ari mu kinyegero kubera yagirizwa kugira uruhara mu bikorwa vyo guhungabanya inzego z'igihugu n'umugambi wo guhungabanya akarere ka Teso."

Mu ndwi iheze, Kainerugaba yagirije Elwelu kwegeranya ibirwanisho no gutunganya ibikorwa vyo kurwanya reta.

Yategetse uwo yahoze ari icegera c'umukuru wa gisirikare kwishikana ku nzego z'umutekano, yongera agabisha ko umuntu wese yomunyegeza azohura n'"ingaruka zikomeye".

Kainerugaba, umuhungu wa Perezida Yoweri Museveni akaba n'umukuru w'igisirikare ca Uganda, yagize ati: "Twarafatiye ibirwanisho n'amasasu vyinshi mu nzu yiwe. Afise amasaha makeyi yo kwishikana ku nzego z'umutekano imbere y'uko tumwita umugarariji, tugahangana na we nk'uko nyene."

Yavuze kandi ko abantu 20 bahoze mu gisirikare bakekwa kuba bafitaniye isano na Elwelu bafashwe.

Umuryango wa Elwelu warahakanye ivyo yagirizwa.

Umukenyezi wiwe, Patricia Apolot, yabwiye ibimenyeshamakuru vyo muri Uganda ko umugabo wiwe ata caha afise, kandi ko atokwiyumvira na rimwe gutanguza ibikorwa vy'ubugarariji.

Apolot yavuze ati: "Akunda Uganda, kandi indoto yiwe ni ukubona igihugu kirangwamwo amahoro."

Naseem Akhtar yakuriye mu mujyi wa Coventry, aho we n'umuryango we bahuraga n'ivangura ndetse no gucirwa imanza n'abandi bantu bitewe n'imiterere y'uruhu rwabo.

Nubwo bakomoka mu muryango w'Abanyapakisitani, indwara y'uruhu rwera (Albinism) iri mu muryango wabo. Ababyeyi be bombi, abana babo batandatu, barimo na Naseem ubwe, ndetse n'abandi bavandimwe babo batandukanye, bose bafite iyi miterere iterwa n'uturemangingo ndangasano (genes).

Albinism ni imiterere ituma umubiri udakora neza umusemburo witwa Melanin, utuma uruhu, umusatsi n'amaso bigira ibara. Ibi bishobora kugira ingaruka ku bushobozi bwo kureba ndetse no ku isura y'umuntu uyifite.

Ibi bituma abagize uyu muryango bagira uruhu rwera cyane n'umusatsi w'umweru. Akhtar yavuze ko ibyo byatumye bagirirwa nabi n'abandi bantu.

Yagize ati: "Nakundaga kwanga aho batwika ibishashi mu ijoro ry'ibirori (Bonfire Night), kuko wabaga uzi neza ko ibishashi bize kunyura mu mwenge w'umuryango w'inzu bakabiduteraho."

Mu myaka ya za 1980, igihe yakuriraga muri uyu mujyi, Akhtar yavuze ko ubuzima butari bworoshye.

Yagize ati: "Igihe navukaga, ivangura n'imyumvire mibi ku bantu bafite ubu bumuga byari bikomeye cyane. Ntekereza ko byari byaranagize ingaruka zikomeye ku babyeyi banjye, ndetse na marume na masenge bari bafite ubu bumuga, kuko bo bavukiye muri Pakisitani. Baje gutura i Coventry bafite imyaka 11 na 12.

"Ntushobora kwihisha ngo abantu batakubona. Ahantu hose uri, mu muryango uwo ari wo wose, abantu barakubona kandi ukagaragara ko utandukanye n'abandi. Ibyo bisaba imbaraga nyinshi n'ubutwari kugira ngo ubashe kwiyakira, kumva ko uri uw'agaciro no gukura wiyizera."

"Ndibwira ko ihungabana tugira tukiri abana bitewe no kutiyakira no kutumva ko turi abo turi bo, bishobora gukomeza kutugiraho ingaruka no mu buzima bwacu bw'ahazaza.

"Ugomba gushaka uburyo bwo guhangana n'amarangamutima.... Iyo ukiri umwana ugenda uhura n'itotezwa kubera ko ugaragara mu buryo butandukanye n'abandi, umubiri n'ubwonko byawe bishobora kumenyera guhora wumva ko uri mu kaga."

Nubwo yahuye n'izo ngorane, Akhtar avuga ko kuva akiri muto yari afite intego yo kumenyekanisha no gusobanurira abantu ibyerekeye Albinism.

"Igihe nari mfite imyaka igera kuri 11, nagiye kuri radiyo yo mu gace k'iwacu kugira ngo mvuge ku bijyanye na Albinism. Nabikoze kuko nifuzaga guhindura imyumvire abantu bari badufiteho, kugira ngo bareke kudufata nk'umuryango bashobora guhohotera cyangwa gutoteza uko bishakiye."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Akhtar arusha imyaka 14 murumuna we Mohammed Rafi, ubu ufite imyaka 32. Yavuze ko uburyo Rafi yakiriwe n'abantu akura bwari butandukanye cyane n'ubwo we yakiriweho.

Rafi yagize ati: "Twakomeje gutura mu gace kamwe ka Coventry, bityo abaturanyi bacu n'abaturage bo muri ako gace baratuzi. Mu myaka yakurikiyeho, abantu bagiye barushaho kumenya no gusobanukirwa n'ubu bumuga."

Akhtar yongeyeho ati: "Ibyo bigaragaza ko ibintu byagiye bihinduka kandi bigatera imbere. Kuba ubuzima Rafi yanyuzemo butandukanye cyane n'ubwo nanyuzemo, bigaragaza ko twe nk'umuryango mugari tugenda turushaho kwakira abantu bafite imiterere itandukanye n'iy'abandi, kandi ko tugenda turushaho kwisanga gake gake."

Rafi ufite ikibazo cyo kutabona neza yongeyeho ati: "Ikintu nyamukuru kiduteza ingorane ni ikibazo cyo kutabona neza."

Nk'uko ikigo cy'ubuzima cy'u Bwongereza (NHS) kibivuga, igabanuka ry'umusemburo wa Melanin ku bantu bafite Albinism rishobora gutera ibibazo bitandukanye by'amaso, birimo: Kutabona neza. Astigmatism: ikibazo cy'amaso gituma umuntu abona ibintu bitagaragara neza bitewe n'imiterere idasanzwe y'ijisho, cyangwa akaba yagira Photophobia: kumva ububabare cyangwa kutihanganira urumuri rwinshi. .

Mu mwaka wa 2022, aba bavandimwe bahawe igihembo cya Guinness World Records kubera kuba ari bo bavandimwe benshi bo mu muryango umwe bafite Albinism.

Akhtar yavuze ko iki gihembo cyari ubutumwa bukomeye bugaragaza ko "ntacyo bitwaye kuba umuntu atandukanye n'abandi, kuko buri wese afite uburenganzira bwo kuba uko ari."

Nta mwana n'umwe mu bana babo ufite Albinism, ariko bose batwaye uturemangingo ndangasano (genes)

Aba bavandimwe bavuze ko batababajwe n'uko iyi miterere ishobora kurangirira ku gisekuru cy'abana babo, ntikomeze kugaragara mu bisekuru bizaza.

Akhtar yagize ati: "Nubwo dufite iyi miterere idutandukanya n'abandi, tunazi ingorane twanyuzemo kugira ngo tubashe kubona uko tubaho no kumenyera kubaho muri ubu buryo budasanzwe.

"Abana bacu bo ntibazahura n'ingorane zo kugira ubumuga cyangwa indwara y'igihe kirekire. Ntekereza ko ari umugisha.

"Nubwo twize kwiyakira kubo turi bo.. Bisaba imbaraga n'umuhate ngo ubashe kwishimira uruhu rwawe."

Akhtar yongeyeho ko binyuze mu gusobanurira abantu ibyerekeye Albinism, yiringiraga ko azafasha ibisekuru bizaza by'abantu bafite ubu bumuga.

Ati: "Dushobora kuvuganira abantu bafite ubu bumuga, tukabaha ijwi kandi tugafasha guhindura imyumvire ya sosiyete."Ibyinshi bishingira ku buryo wowe ubwawe wibona. Uko ugenda uhindura imyumvire ufite kuri wowe ubwawe, ni ko ubuzima bwawe bushobora kurushaho kuba bwiza.

"Igihe nari nkiri umwana, hari umuntu wambereye isoko y'ihumure. Yari umwarimu wihariye wazaga kumfasha igihe nari nkiri muto, kandi na we yari afite Albinism.

"Yarandemeye kandi ambera urugero rwiza. Bityo, niba nanjye nk'umuntu nshobora kugira icyo natanga ku iyi si, nkaba isoko y'ihumure n'ihirwe ku bandi, numva ko nzaba nasohoje inshingano zanjye kuri iyi si."

US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.

He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.

The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.

In a letter to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump said Pretoria's actions on international security and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to Washington risked undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.

He also accused South Africa of maintaining significant barriers to American trade and investment, including restrictions affecting agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections and intellectual property.

"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.

"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC

Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims?

South Africa has also sought to put the potential impact of losing Agoa benefits into perspective, arguing that the country's broader trade relationship with the US extends well beyond the programme.

Government figures show that about 89% of South African exports to the US entered under ordinary World Trade Organization most-favoured-nation terms in 2025, while around 10% benefited from Agoa, down from 28% in 2024.

"The value of South African exports under the programme fell to about $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in 2025, from $4bn the previous year," Tau said.

Bilateral trade between the two countries reached $28.8bn in 2025, while more than 600 American companies operate in South Africa, supporting about 134,600 jobs.

Pretoria says the two economies have complementary trade interests. South Africa supplies 12 of the 50 minerals considered critical by the US, as well as 70% of American isotopes used, among other things, in cancer treatment.

South African manufacturers also use American inputs in products exported to the US under Agoa, including vehicles and boats.

Oxford Economics senior economist Jee-A van der Linde said Washington's move will put further pressure on South Africa's manufacturing sector, warning that affected exports may be difficult to redirect to other markets.

"This decision comes as global trade flows remained disrupted and South Africa faces growing competition from cheap Chinese imports, particularly in the automotive industry," he said.

However, he noted that South Africa had previously managed to redirect some tariff-affected exports to markets including Europe and China.

US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.

"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.

Last year, Trump accused South Africa of persecuting its white minority and launched a programme for white Afrikaners to get asylum in the US.

Trump also repeated widely discredited claims of a genocide of South Africa's white population.

In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.

The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo .

The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

Rwanda has denied backing the M23 despite overwhelming evidence.

Rwanda saw its exports to the US rise to $43.3 million in 2025, up from $13.1 million in 2024, according to US import data.

Alexander Venter, an Oxford Economics economist, said Washington accounted for about 2% of Rwanda's merchandise exports in 2025, with only around 4% of its exports to the US benefiting from Agoa preferences.

Neighbouring African countries and Asian markets continued to dominate Rwanda's trade, Venter added.

Nike clothes are popular in Libya, although many are counterfeit

Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo.

The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings.

It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god.

Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name.

The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

It referred to a statement issued by its Council for Research and Sharia Studies on 5 November 2023, urging Muslims to boycott Western companies it considers supportive of Israel during the war in Gaza.

The ruling, known as a fatwa, is a religious opinion on a matter of Islamic law. It was approved by Libya's Grand Mufti, Sadiq al-Gharyani.

The Dar al-Ifta is an influential religious institution based in Tripoli, in western Libya. The country is politically divided, with rival authorities and institutions operating in the east and west after years of conflict following the toppling of long-time leader Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Although its religious rulings can carry considerable social influence, they are not necessarily government orders or legally enforceable.

Last year it ruled against wearing jewellery and watches bearing the logo of French luxury jewellery house Van Cleef & Arpels, arguing that its four-leaf clover design was associated with Christian beliefs and the pursuit of good luck, which it said contradicted Islamic teachings.

The latest fatwa does not announce a state ban on Nike products or specify penalties for people who continue to buy or wear them.

Social media reactions were mixed, with some users welcoming the ruling, while others questioned its significance, describing it as ironic or a distraction from more pressing issues.

The ruling comes amid wider debates over the rise of religious conservatism in public life in Libya.

In 2025, authorities in eastern Libya announced restrictions on rap music, theatre and dance performances, citing concerns that some lyrics and performances violated public morals and Islamic values.

The measures were subsequently extended to western Libya.

The Dar al-Ifta has also previously issued religious rulings against music, although there is no clear evidence that it was directly involved in the restrictions on performances.

Nike does not operate an official store in Libya, however Nike-branded products are available through local sportswear retailers.

Sportswear brands such as Nike and Adidas are popular across North Africa.

In Libya, as in other countries in the region, counterfeit versions of popular sportswear brands are also sold in local markets.

Uganda accuses Peter Elwelu of stockpiling weapons and organising activities against the government

Uganda has arrested former deputy military chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu over allegations of involvement in activities aimed at destabilising the country.

Acting military spokesman Chris Magezi said Elwelu, whom he described as a "renegade" officer, was arrested on Monday evening and would be charged in court.

The arrest comes days after Uganda's defence chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, announced that he had stripped Elwelu of his lieutenant general rank and demoted him to a private.

Elwelu has not commented on the allegations.

Elwelu rose to prominence in 2016 when he oversaw a deadly military raid on the palace of a regional king accused of leading a separatist movement. He was subsequently appointed army chief.

He later rose to become the deputy chief of defence forces before being named presidential adviser.

In May 2024, the US government imposed sanctions on him over alleged human rights abuses, including extrajudicial killings committed by government forces. He retired from the military in August 2025.

On Monday, the military spokesman said security forces had recently recovered 15 guns in his possession, military fatigues, and two pick-up trucks.

"Elwelu has been on the run over involvement in subversive activities and plans to destabilise Teso," Magezi said, referring to an area in eastern Uganda.

Last week, Kainerugaba accused Elwelu of stockpiling weapons and organising activities against the government.

He ordered the former army boss to surrender, warning that anyone helping him evade arrest would face "serious consequences".

"We have recovered a lot of arms and ammunition from his house. He has hours to surrender before we declare him a rebel and deal with him," said Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni, as well as being the country's defence chief.

He also said that 20 former soldiers allegedly linked to Elwelu had been arrested.

Elwelu's family has rejected the allegations.

His wife, Patricia Apolot, told local media that her husband was innocent and could not contemplate starting a rebellion.

"He loves Uganda, and his dream is to have a peaceful country," Apolot said.
