MN202611_1r868nmz54g.t:
Morocco claims Western Sahara as part of its territory

Morocco has welcomed the end of a decades-long UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a diplomatic showdown between the US and Russia left the Security Council unable to agree on its future.

The council failed on Friday to renew the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (Minurso) after Russia vetoed a US-backed proposal. A rival Russian draft to extend the mission also failed to secure enough votes.

The decision raises questions about the future of Africa's longest territorial dispute and the fragile ceasefire between Morocco, which claims Western Sahara, and the Polisario Front which has been fighting for the territory's independence for more than 50 years.

Western Sahara, on Africa's north-west coast, was a Spanish colony until 1975. It has significant phosphate reserves and valuable fishing grounds along its Atlantic coast.

As Spain prepared to withdraw, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory.

The International Court of Justice found historical ties of allegiance but no territorial sovereignty that overrode the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination.

Morocco's then King Hassan II responded by organising the Green March. On 6 November 1975 about 350,000 Moroccan civilians entered the territory in a mass demonstration intended to put pressure on Spain.

Days later, Spain signed the Madrid Accords with Morocco and Mauritania, agreeing to transfer administrative control. Morocco took the northern two-thirds and Mauritania the southern third. The agreement did not settle the question of sovereignty.

The Polisario Front, an independence movement founded in 1973, opposed the deal. It saw it as replacing Spanish colonial rule with Moroccan and Mauritanian control.

Mauritania renounced its claim in 1979, but Morocco continued fighting Polisario.

Algeria became Polisario's main regional ally, providing military support and hosting its leadership and thousands of Sahrawi refugees in camps near the city of Tindouf.

The North African country says its position is based on the right to self-determination, while Morocco sees Western Sahara as an integral part of its territory.

Morocco and Algeria fought a brief border war in 1963 over disagreements about territory inherited from French colonial rule. Their relationship has remained tense, with Western Sahara at the centre of their dispute.

After 16 years of fighting, Morocco and Polisario agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991, with the territory divided by a sand wall, or berm, to keep the rival forces apart.

The UN established Minurso to monitor the ceasefire and organise a referendum on the territory's future. Sahrawis were meant to choose between independence and integration with Morocco.

The vote was scheduled for 1992 but never took place. The two sides could not agree on who would be eligible to participate, with disputes over voter identification becoming a major obstacle.

In 2007, Morocco put forward a proposal for autonomy, which would see Sahrawis managing their internal affairs, while Rabat retained control over defence and foreign relations.

Thousands of Moroccans marched into Western Sahara in 1975 in what became known as the Green March

The Polisario Front and Algeria rejected the plan, insisting on a referendum that included independence as an option.

Years of UN-sponsored negotiations failed to produce a breakthrough.

The ceasefire broke down in November 2020, when Polisario said it was resuming armed struggle.

But following a long diplomatic campaign by Morocco, the UN Security Council voted in 2025 in favour of a resolution backing the autonomy plan as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.

While most Sahrawis live in the part of Western Sahara controlled by Morocco, tens of thousands are estimated to be in refugee camps in Algeria.

The US proposed extending Minurso's mandate for another year, but its draft went beyond the usual renewal.

It would have removed the word "referendum" from the mission's name and made Morocco's autonomy proposal the sole basis for further negotiations.

The draft received the support of 11 of the Security Council's 15 members, including France and the UK but Russia vetoed it, arguing that it was too favourable to Morocco.

Russia then proposed extending Minurso's mandate without changing its terms. That draft also failed, receiving only two votes in favour.

Minurso's mandate expired at the end of Saturday, 31 October. The UN said the following day that the mission had entered a liquidation period, with a reduced team overseeing the transfer of military equipment and other assets.

The UN mission has been in Western Sahara since 1991

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the Sahrawi people's right to self-determination must be respected and warned of the risk of renewed hostilities.

The Polisario Front condemned the US proposal. Its representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing it, saying it would "torpedo the foundations of the UN peace process" and threaten regional and international peace.

Morocco, meanwhile, said the mission's personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days, arguing that Western Sahara issue should no longer be considered by the Security Council.

Minurso had 155 military personnel and was expected to cost $62m (£46m) in the financial year beginning in June, according to a UN report.

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew Minurso's mandate.

In Laayoune, the territory's largest city, footage showed people celebrating, waving Moroccan flags and displaying portraits of King Mohammed VI.

"The decision is an opportunity for Rabat to challenge what it sees as an international mechanism that has failed to resolve the dispute," Issam Laaroussi, a Moroccan expert in international relations, tells the BBC.

He said Morocco would now have more room to push its autonomy proposal and shift negotiations away from a referendum on independence towards autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty.

The decision does not, however, change Western Sahara's legal status or amount to international recognition of Moroccan sovereignty.

Western Sahara remains on the UN list of non-self-governing territories, while the African Union officially recognises its independence, as the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR).

But the decision comes after several countries backed the position of Morocco, which in recent years has made securing international support for its claim a central part of its foreign policy.

In 2020, the US recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara as part of an agreement to establish diplomatic relations between Morocco and Israel.

France also backed Morocco's autonomy plan as the basis for resolving the dispute in 2024.

Thousands of Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Algeria

Morocco rejoined the African Union in 2017, more than three decades after leaving its predecessor, the Organisation of African Unity, in protest at the SADR's admission.

Since returning, Rabat has sought to build support for its position from within the organisation. At least 10 African countries have opened diplomatic missions in the territory in support of Rabat.

"Morocco is not necessarily seeking to abandon the UN process, but to change the framework for negotiations and draw greater support from regional organisations," says Laaroussi.

Addressing a special joint session of parliament on Monday, House of Representatives Speaker Ahmed Touizi hailed the end of Minurso as a victory for the country's diplomacy.

He said the country should now move from "managing the dispute to implementing its autonomy plan under Moroccan sovereignty, while pressing ahead with development projects in the territory."

The fear is that Minurso's departure could lead to renewed fighting.

The mission has monitored military developments and helped reduce the risk of escalation.

Aid organisation Oxfam warned that losing its monitoring and de-escalation role could undermine stability, with serious consequences for civilians.

Laaroussi admits that the mission's departure could create security gaps.

"Minurso's departure does not create the original conflict, because the conflict is already there, but it could aggravate an already fragile security environment," he says.

The UN decision has also fuelled nationalist rhetoric online.

Several Moroccan users have shared AI-generated images of themselves in military uniform, declaring their readiness to fight for Morocco's sovereignty over Western Sahara.

In Morocco, Western Sahara is widely regarded as a national cause. Political parties that are often divided on other issues are united in supporting the country's claim to sovereignty over the territory.

Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita has said the end of the mission does not mean the end of the ceasefire, and that Rabat remains committed to it "within respect of its security and sovereignty."

Polisario has not said what it will do next.

Any resumption of fighting could well draw in Algeria, as tensions with Morocco remain high.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), both countries significantly increased military spending last year, with SIPRI citing their dispute over Western Sahara as a key driver.

Algeria spent an estimated $25.4bn, more than four time Morocco's $6.3bn.

Donovan Marx's family and officals have welcomed the swift arrests of suspects linked to the farm attack

Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressing

Four people have been charged with attempted murder in South Africa over a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.

Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.

Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.

Five people were arrested over the weekend but only four appeared in court on Tuesday.

The suspects, aged between 26 and 56, were charged with attempted murder, robbery and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition.

The fifth suspect has since turned state witness, the North West police chief confirmed on Tuesday.

The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.

Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.

A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.

The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.

When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.

"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."

The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.

The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.

Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.

South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".

The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.

Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.

Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.

South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.

However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

KIGALI – Clement Uwajeneza, the former Chief Executive Officer of Irembo, has taken over the leadership of Rwanda’s Private Sector Federation (PSF), succeeding Callixte Kanamugire, who had been serving as Acting Chief Executive Officer.

Uwajeneza formally assumed office on November 3, 2026, bringing an experience in technology, digital transformation and business management to an organization representing the country’s business community.

Following a leadership handover ceremony at PSF headquarters in Kigali, the transition also saw the formal introduction of André Gashugi as the Federation’s new Deputy Chief Executive Officer.

Uwajeneza joins PSF after serving as Chief Operating Officer at NewGlobe, where he led teams operating across six countries in efforts to transform public education through digitalization and structured pedagogy.

He previously headed Irembo, the company behind Rwanda’s digital government services platform, and served as Country Director of Andela Rwanda. He is also a former Chairperson of the Rwanda ICT Chamber.

His appointment brings experience in technology entrepreneurship and digital business development to an institution whose mandate includes representing businesses, promoting entrepreneurship and strengthening private-sector competitiveness.

Speaking after his appointment, Uwajeneza said he intended to work closely with the Federation’s members, leadership, staff and stakeholders to strengthen the organization’s institutional capacity and advance the interests of businesses.

His immediate challenge will be to lead an organization whose members operate across different sectors and face a range of concerns, including access to markets, financing, business regulation and competitiveness.

The importance of these challenges was highlighted during the opening of the 26th East African Community Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Trade Fair in Kigali, where Antoine Kajangwe, Rwanda’s Minister of Trade and Industry, called on regional businesses to take greater advantage of opportunities created by economic integration.

“MSMEs are the backbone of East Africa’s economy. They create a large share of our jobs, supply our markets, carry the entrepreneurial energy of our people,” Kajangwe said.

The Minister, however, cautioned that businesses could not fully benefit from the regional market without addressing barriers that continue to constrain cross-border trade.

“A market is only as open as its borders. Enterprises should build their capacity to compete within the East African Community and eventually across the wider African Continental Free Trade Area,” he said.

Investment and Institutional Management Experience

Callixte Kanamugire, who had been serving as Acting Chief Executive Officer.

Gashugi, brings more than 15 years of experience in financial services, investment management, strategic planning and institutional development. He is the founding CEO of the Rwanda National Investment Trust (RNIT), which was establish in 2014.

He subsequently served as Chief Operations Officer and Chief Investment Officer, contributing to the management and investment of a portfolio valued at approximately RWF200 billion.

At RNIT, he also contributed to the launch of the Iterambere Fund and the institution’s investment operations, maintaining clean audit reports during his tenure, according to PSF.

Before joining RNIT, Gashugi worked at the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda, where he served as Director of Administration, Logistics and Human Resources, overseeing institutional operations, budgets and organizational development.

At the handover ceremony, PSF First Vice-Chairperson Jean Claude Uwizeyemungu said the transition reflected the Federation’s commitment to institutional continuity and governance.

“This leadership transition reflects PSF’s commitment to institutional continuity, strong governance and sustained progress in advancing Rwanda’s private sector,” he said.

The PSF serves as the principal platform for private-sector representation and public-private dialogue, with responsibility for strengthening the business environment and ensuring that the concerns of enterprises are reflected in national economic discussions.

MN202611_45bs4iiv40.t:
Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva wants inspecting stalls at the 26th East African Community (EAC) Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) Trade Fair in Kigali.

KIGALI – East Africa needs nearly 290 million pairs of shoes every year, but manufacturers across the region produce only about 17 million. That gap is an opportunity for the region’s small businesses to grow into industries capable of supplying a much larger market.

Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva wants small businesses to be part of that transformation, not remain confined to the modest production levels at which many currently operate.

At the 26th East African Community (EAC) Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) Trade Fair in Kigali, he cited a Rwandan shoe manufacturer with an annual capacity of 6,000 pairs, an example of enterprises that could grow with the right support.

The 26th East African Community (EAC) MSMEs Trade Fair is also known as the Jua Kali / Nguvu Kazi Exhibition.

“We want these MSMEs to grow up. We want you to be billionaires, and we are here to help. Government institutions and financial partners are ready to help small enterprises expand their capacity and take advantage of the wider regional market,” Nsengiyumva told exhibitors.

The fair, running from October 30 to November 8 under the theme Advancing Regional Value Chains in Leather and Horticulture, has brought together 1,500 exhibitors from across East Africa and beyond.

Its focus reflects two sectors with considerable potential to create jobs, strengthen regional production and reduce reliance on imported finished goods.

Available statistics indicate that regional demand for footwear rose from 130 million pairs in 2017 to nearly 290 million in 2024, while local production stood at about 17 million pairs. Demand is projected to reach 385 million pairs by 2030.

With the challenge to connect that demand to businesses able to produce competitively at scale, Nsengiyumva called for greater investment in processing, footwear manufacturing and finished leather products, rather than allowing the region’s hides and skins to leave as raw materials.

The growth of MSMEs is link to Rwanda’s wider economic ambitions, including the creation of 250,000 jobs annually and increasing non-traditional exports from US$1.4 billion to US$3.2 billion over five years.

In horticulture, the PM highlighted the need for better storage, cold-chain facilities, packaging, processing and distribution to help producers reach larger markets.

From National Exhibitions to Regional Value Chains

EAC Deputy Secretary General in charge of Customs, Trade and Monetary Affairs, Annette Mutawawe addressing exhibitors.

For the first time, exhibitors at the fair have been grouped by economic sector rather than by country, an arrangement intended to encourage partnerships among businesses working in the same value chains across national borders.

EAC Deputy Secretary General in charge of Customs, Trade and Monetary Affairs, Annette Mutawawe said the change marked a shift from simply displaying products towards building commercial relationships that could strengthen regional production.

“We are moving from showcasing products primarily by country to connecting businesses by sector. From individual national exhibitions to opportunities for regional collaboration and from displaying products to creating stronger regional value chains,” she noted.

Agriculture contributes more than a quarter of the EAC’s combined GDP, while leather and horticulture offer opportunities to connect farmers, processors, manufacturers, distributors and retailers across partner states.

The success of that integration, however, also depends on whether businesses can move goods efficiently and access markets beyond their home countries.

Mutawawe said border crossing times had been reduced by up to 70 per cent, while transit time under the single customs territory had fallen from 18 days to four. She also cited a 44 per cent increase in EAC exports to the rest of Africa, which reached US$7.2 billion.

The effort to expand regional trade is also placing greater emphasis on women entrepreneurs, whose participation is essential to making integration more inclusive.

Sixteen women from the eight Partner States were recognized as champion mentees under the EAC Women in Trade Champions Initiative, a six-month program designed to strengthen their understanding of regional trade policies, market opportunities and cross-border procedures.

The initiative reflects a broader ambition to move women beyond participation in local commerce and equip them to build businesses that can compete across the regional market.

As Mutawawe put it, the goal is for East Africans to increasingly consume products made within the region and support businesses that operate across national boundaries.

“Our task is to ensure that the next generation of East Africans wear shoes made in East Africa, eat foods processed in East Africa and build businesses that cross every border in East Africa and beyond,” she remarked.

Dr Caroline Asiimwe, Executive Secretary and CEO of the East African Kiswahili Commission speaking to the media.

Access to markets depends on more than roads, customs systems and finance. Businesses must also be able to communicate with customers, suppliers and institutions in other countries.

Dr Caroline Asiimwe, Executive Secretary and CEO of the East African Kiswahili Commission, said language remains an important part of regional integration, particularly for small traders who need to understand customs requirements, tariffs, trade procedures and information from EAC institutions.

“Traders need to understand the policies, the procedures and the information that govern regional trade. Without effective communication, they cannot fully take advantage of the opportunities created by regional integration,” she said.

Kiswahili’s adoption as an official EAC language alongside English provides a foundation for wider communication, but more needs to be done to make regional trade information accessible to people in languages they understand.

The Commission is exploring digital innovations, including artificial intelligence, to help traders access information and services across language barriers.

Asiimwe warned that African languages risk being left out of the digital ecosystem unless institutions invest in their development and use.

For the small manufacturers and producers, the immediate opportunity lies in turning regional demand into orders, investment and expanded production. The wider goal is to make East Africa a market in which its own businesses can supply more of what its people consume.

MN202611_f1d60o857a.t:
Nuwagaba Issac and Mugisha Fred (in Red)

KIGALI – Two Ugandan nationals are among 11 people arrested in Rwanda over the theft and destruction of electricity infrastructure, including copper power cables, in a criminal operation linked to intermittent power outages in different parts of the country.

The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) presented the suspects to the media on Tuesday, November 3, following joint operations with the Rwanda National Police.

The two Ugandan nationals have been identified as Nuwagaba Isaac and Mugisha Fred. They are accused of buying stolen electricity cables from members of the group and arranging their sale outside Rwanda.

RIB spokesperson Dr. Thierry Murangira B. said the suspects operated as an organised network, with different members playing specific roles in stealing, transporting and selling the cables.

Some members allegedly stole the cables from electricity infrastructure, while others bought, transported and prepared them for resale. The network reportedly included motorcycle taxi operators and drivers who helped move the stolen materials.

One of the Ugandan suspects was described as a key trader who would take the stolen cables across the border for sale in other countries.

More than one tonne of stolen cables recovered

During the operation, investigators recovered approximately 1.5 tonnes of copper electricity cables valued at about Rwf20 million.

The cables were allegedly stolen from several districts, including Gasabo, Kicukiro, Nyarugenge, Kamonyi and Bugesera.

Authorities link the group’s activities to repeated power interruptions recently experienced in different parts of Rwanda, following the theft and destruction of electricity infrastructure.

The arrests were made in different locations, mainly in Kigali and neighbouring districts.

The 11 suspects face three charges: forming or participating in a criminal gang, theft and destruction of infrastructure.

Under Rwanda’s criminal law, stealing electricity cables carries a potential prison sentence of between three and five years.

RIB said the case files had been forwarded to the Prosecution for further legal proceedings.

The suspects are being held at RIB detention facilities in Nyarugenge and Kicukiro.

The investigation comes amid concerns over the damage and theft of critical public infrastructure, which can disrupt essential services and impose additional costs on electricity distribution and maintenance.

The Rwanda Investigation Bureau (RIB) has recovered Rwf23 million out of Rwf28 million suspected to have been embezzled in a corruption case involving public officials and other individuals in Gisagara District, as the agency separately announced the arrest of 11 people suspected of vandalising critical infrastructure, particularly electricity cables.

RIB spokesperson Dr Murangira B. Thierry disclosed the recovery on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, revealing that the money was allegedly misappropriated by individuals including Gisagara District Deputy Mayor in charge of Social Affairs, Dusabe Denise, the district’s Director of Criminal Investigations (DCI), and Catholic priest Father Kayumba Maurice.

The recovery represents the bulk of the Rwf28 million under investigation, leaving Rwf5 million yet to be accounted for.

In a separate case, RIB presented 11 suspects to the media over their alleged involvement in the destruction and theft of public infrastructure, with investigators estimating the value of the stolen property at approximately Rwf20 million.

The suspects are accused of three offences: forming or joining a criminal gang, damaging infrastructure and theft.

According to RIB, the alleged criminal activities mainly targeted electricity infrastructure, including power cables, raising concerns over the security of essential public utilities and the potential disruption of electricity services.

The 11 suspects are currently detained at RIB stations in Nyarugenge and Kicukiro as investigations continue.

The cases highlight RIB’s ongoing efforts to tackle corruption, protect public infrastructure and bring individuals suspected of economic and other criminal offences to justice.

He reaffirmed the RDF’s commitment to sharing its experience and expertise with friendly armed forces as part of collective efforts to promote peace, security and stability across the African continent.

Gen MAMADOU, the FACA Chief of General Staff, expressed his sincere appreciation to the Government of Rwanda, the RDF leadership and the instructors for their commitment, professionalism and dedication throughout the training period.

He emphasised that the skills, discipline and knowledge acquired by their personnel would enhance their ability to fulfil their duties effectively and contribute to the security and stability of the Central African Republic.

The graduation marks an important milestone in the professional development of FACA personnel and underscores the longstanding defence cooperation between Rwanda and the Central African Republic, particularly in military training, capacity-building and professional development.

The government of Rwanda has secured a U$4.97Million from the Adaptation Fund to strengthen climate resilience among smallholder farmers in Kayonza,Gatsibo and Nyagatare districts.

The project aims at improving access to climate information and climate-smart farming technologies,benefiting at least 10,000 farmers.

This UNDP-Ministry of Agriculture project seeks to promote climate-smart agriculture, improving advisory services and reducing losses from drought and erratic rainfall.

According to details the Adaptation Fund has approved nearly U$35 million for climate resilience in Rwanda and the Horn of Africa, including U$4.97 million for Rwanda and U$30 million for drought-affected communities in Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia.

Adaptation Fund finances projects and programmes that help vulnerable communities in developing countries adapt to climate change.

Initiatives are based on country needs, views and priorities.

Climate change is predicted to greatly affect the poorest people in the world, who are often hardest hit by weather catastrophes, desertification, and rising sea levels, yet have contributed the least to the problem of global warming.

Since 2010, the Adaptation Fund has committed about 1.6 billion for climate change adaptation and resilience projects and programmes, including 226 concrete, localized projects in the most vulnerable communities of developing countries around the world with about 120 million total beneficiaries.

It also pioneered Direct Access and Enhanced Direct Access, empowering countries to access funding and develop local projects directly through accredited national implementing entities.

President Paul Kagame has held separate meetings with Jamaican Prime Minister Andrew Holness and World Trade Organization (WTO) Director-General Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala on the sidelines of the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM 2026) in Antigua and Barbuda, focusing on strengthening bilateral relations, expanding trade and attracting investment.

The discussions reflect Rwanda’s efforts to deepen international partnerships, promote economic cooperation and identify new opportunities for sustainable development.

During his meeting with Prime Minister Holness, Kagame discussed the longstanding cooperation between Rwanda and Jamaica, exploring ways to expand collaboration in areas of mutual interest, including health, defence and tourism.

The two leaders examined the potential to build on existing relations by strengthening cooperation in sectors that could support economic development, improve public services and create opportunities for citizens of both countries.

Kagame’s engagement with Holness also highlights Rwanda’s interest in broadening partnerships beyond traditional diplomatic relationships and developing practical cooperation with countries that share common development priorities.

In a separate meeting, Kagame held discussions with WTO Director-General Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala on Rwanda’s ongoing partnership with the global trade body and the importance of strengthening regional trade and investment.

The talks centred on the role of trade in driving sustainable development, with greater regional integration and investment seen as important avenues for expanding economic opportunities.

For Rwanda, stronger engagement with the WTO and regional trading partners is particularly important in supporting market access for local businesses, encouraging investment and enabling producers to reach wider markets.

The discussions also come amid broader efforts to strengthen economic cooperation among Commonwealth member states, where trade, investment and partnerships are key priorities for accelerating development.

Through the two engagements, Rwanda is seeking to consolidate existing diplomatic relationships while advancing economic partnerships that can deliver tangible benefits in health, tourism, trade and investment.

CHOGM 2026 brings together leaders from across the Commonwealth to discuss shared challenges and opportunities, strengthen cooperation and explore strategies for promoting inclusive growth and prosperity among member countries.

Agriculture plays a vital role in Africa’s economic development, supporting rural livelihoods, creating jobs and sustaining food security.

Yet, farmers and agricultural businesses continue to face challenges ranging from limited market access and investment to climate-related disasters that can undo years of progress.

Addressing these issues requires sound economic policies, stronger regional partnerships and practical solutions that help communities grow and withstand uncertainty.

‎At the centre of this work is Ngabitsinze Jean Chrysostome, Director General of African Risk Capacity (ARC) Group, whose experience spans applied economics, agricultural research and public policymaking.

His professional journey has been shaped by a clear understanding of how agricultural productivity, market opportunities and economic resilience influence people’s lives.

Through his academic work, he has explored ways to improve production efficiency, strengthen agricultural value chains and expand market access for smallholder farmers, with the wider aim of supporting rural development and food security.

‎His experience in government has further shaped his approach to economic development.

Working across agriculture and trade, he has supported policies aimed at attracting investment, expanding exports and reducing dependence on imports.

He also recognises the importance of private sector participation and regional value chains in creating stronger, more resilient economies.

His engagement with continental and international platforms, including the Commonwealth Trade Ministers’ Meeting and initiatives aligned with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), reflects his belief that cooperation is essential to unlocking Africa’s economic potential.

‎Today, at ARC, he brings these experiences together to advance disaster preparedness, strengthen financial protection and help African countries safeguard the livelihoods and development gains of their people.

‎A Career Shaped by Economic Development

‎Ngabitsinze has built his professional journey around this connection between economic development and resilience.

His background in applied economics, agricultural research and policymaking has given him a practical understanding of the challenges facing farmers and rural economies.

‎His experience in Rwanda showed him how closely agricultural productivity, market access and household security are linked.

It also revealed how quickly climate shocks can reverse years of development.

These experiences shaped his commitment to policies that protect livelihoods while creating opportunities for lasting economic progress.

At ARC, he brings this perspective to the challenge of helping African countries prepare for disasters and respond before their effects become more severe.

‎Strengthening Disaster Preparedness Across Africa

‎As Director General, Ngabitsinze is focused on expanding country participation in ARC, strengthening preparedness and improving access to affordable disaster risk financing.

His priority is to ensure that the institution’s work translates into timely assistance for vulnerable communities.

‎He also recognises that effective disaster management depends on strong institutional relationships.

Transparent decision-making, accountability and constructive dialogue among ARC’s governing bodies, member states and partners are essential to building trust.

In his view, institutional credibility is not simply an administrative matter. It is fundamental to delivering meaningful results.

‎Climate-related disasters can affect entire agricultural systems, disrupting production, reducing household incomes and placing pressure on food supplies.

Ngabitsinze believes countries must connect early warning systems with practical plans and financing that can be accessed before a crisis escalates.

‎Reliable climate information is important, but it must lead to action. Investments in resilient farming, water management, livestock protection and functioning food markets can help communities prepare for changing conditions.

Farmers, pastoralists and fishers should also have a voice in shaping preparedness plans so that support reflects the risks they face in their daily lives.

‎The objective is to help countries act earlier, reducing losses before they become more difficult and expensive to address.

‎Making Disaster Financing More Effective

‎When a disaster strikes, governments must provide immediate assistance while protecting resources needed for long-term development.

Arranging funds only after an emergency can delay relief and place additional pressure on public budgets.

‎Pre-arranged financing offers a more practical approach. Ngabitsinze sees parametric insurance as a useful mechanism because it can release funds when agreed thresholds are met, allowing governments to respond more quickly.

However, insurance works best as part of a wider strategy that includes reserves, contingency credit and social protection.

‎The real measure of success is whether financial support reaches affected communities in time to protect lives and livelihoods.

Financing should help governments manage emergencies without sacrificing essential development priorities.

‎Addressing the Challenges Facing Smallholder Farmers

‎Smallholder farmers often face several barriers at once, including limited access to finance, unreliable agricultural inputs, inadequate infrastructure, weak extension services and uncertain markets.

Women and young farmers may face additional difficulties accessing land and productive assets.

‎Ngabitsinze believes these challenges require coordinated solutions.

Better access to finance and inputs must go hand in hand with stronger agricultural advisory services, reliable infrastructure and policies that allow farmers to plan ahead.

Producer organisations can also help farmers improve their bargaining power and reach wider markets.

‎Higher productivity is important, but it must translate into better incomes and more secure livelihoods.

Farmers need commercial opportunities alongside the resources and support required to manage risk.

‎Creating Greater Value Across Agricultural Supply Chains

‎Opportunities to strengthen African agriculture extend beyond the farm. Poor storage, limited processing facilities and weak market connections can reduce the value farmers receive from their produce.

‎Ngabitsinze sees considerable potential in reducing post-harvest losses, expanding storage and cold-chain facilities, supporting local processing and improving access to markets.

These investments can increase farmers’ earnings while creating employment and business opportunities in rural areas.

‎Their success depends on supporting infrastructure, including reliable energy, transport, quality standards and accessible finance.

Agricultural value chains should ultimately be judged by how much value they create for farmers and rural communities, not simply by the volume of produce entering the market.

‎Connecting Research with Practical Results

‎Research in agricultural economics can help identify ways to improve productivity, use resources more efficiently and expand market access.

Its value, however, depends on whether findings lead to practical improvements.

‎Ngabitsinze believes researchers, policymakers, extension services and farmers should work together to identify problems, test solutions and assess their results.

Progress should be measured through changes in farm incomes, productivity, resilience and market participation.

‎He also supports adjusting programmes when evidence shows they are not working as intended.

This willingness to learn and adapt helps ensure that public resources are directed towards interventions that deliver real benefits to farmers and local economies.

‎Climate risks and food markets cross national borders, making cooperation essential to Africa’s long-term food security.

Countries can share forecasting capabilities, strengthen risk models and coordinate disaster preparedness rather than working in isolation.

‎Regional risk pooling can help participating countries spread exposure, while predictable trade can improve the movement of food from areas with available supplies to those experiencing shortages.

‎Ngabitsinze believes regional institutions must turn cooperation into practical services that countries can rely on and sustain.

Stronger partnerships can help African nations manage shared risks while improving their ability to protect agricultural production and food supplies.

‎Balancing Emergency Relief with Long-Term Resilience

‎During a disaster, protecting lives and preventing immediate losses must come first.

Yet, timely assistance can also determine whether families retain the resources needed to rebuild their lives.

‎Without support, households may be forced to sell livestock, use their savings or abandon their livelihoods.

Ngabitsinze believes relief efforts should help families meet urgent needs while protecting their productive assets.

‎Recovery should then focus on rebuilding stronger agricultural systems and infrastructure.

Connecting emergency response with long-term planning allows governments to move beyond immediate relief and reduce vulnerability to future disasters.

‎Using Innovation to Anticipate Climate Risks

‎Satellite observations, improved forecasting, digital payments and more accurate risk models offer new ways to strengthen disaster preparedness.

These tools can help governments understand potential losses, improve decisions and deliver assistance more efficiently.

‎Ngabitsinze stresses that innovation must be supported by reliable local data, accessible services and trusted institutions.

He also highlights basis risk, which occurs when an insurance payout does not adequately reflect the losses people experience.

Improving data quality and insurance design is therefore essential to ensuring that financial protection works as intended.

‎Technology should ultimately be judged by its ability to improve decisions and provide better protection for vulnerable communities.

‎Integrating Agriculture, Finance and Climate Policy

‎Ngabitsinze believes African countries need stronger coordination among finance, agriculture, environment and disaster-management institutions.

Climate risks should inform public investment, agricultural policy and national budgeting rather than being treated as separate concerns.

‎Capable public institutions, effective extension services, transparent financing and dependable social protection are important to this effort.

Development partners can contribute by supporting nationally led strategies with predictable funding and clear accountability.

‎When resilience becomes part of everyday policy and investment decisions, countries are better positioned to protect development gains and prepare for future challenges.

‎Ngabitsinze’s ambition is to help build institutions that enable African countries to anticipate crises, protect development progress and create opportunities for their people.

He sees success in practical terms: farmers investing with greater confidence, governments responding earlier and communities recovering with dignity.

‎His experience in agricultural economics, research and public service has reinforced his belief that development must improve people’s lives.

As climate risks continue to challenge Africa’s food systems and economies, his work at ARC reflects a wider goal of making resilience an integral part of the continent’s development.

The lasting impact will be measured by how well countries protect their people and preserve the progress they have worked hard to achieve.

Paris Jackson, umukobwa w’umuhanzi Michael Jackson, yasabye urukiko gutegeka ko miliyoni 600 z’amadolari ya Amerika ava mu mutungo wa se agashyirwa mu kigega cy’umuryango kigenewe kumufasha na basaza be babiri, Prince na Bigi Jackson.

Paris avuga ko icyo kigega kimaze imyaka irenga 17 kitarashyirwamo n'urupfumuye nyamara umutungo wa se warakomeje kwinjiza amafaranga menshi binyuze mu masezerano akomeye y’ubucuruzi.

Inyandiko y'ubu busabe yagejejwe mu rukiko rw'i Los Angeles igaragaza ko, hakurikijwe gahunda yari yarateganyijwe mu micungire y’umurage wa Michael Jackson, abana be bari kuzajya bahabwa inyungu zituruka ku migabane yabo buri wese amaze kugira imyaka 21.

Paris agaragaza ko iki kibazo gihangayikishije cyane cyane kuko musaza we Prince ari hafi kugira imyaka 30, we akaba azuzuza imyaka 29 muri Mata 2027, mu gihe murumuna wabo Bigi azuzuza imyaka 25 muri Gashyantare 2027.

Michael Jackson yitabye Imana ku wa 25 Kamena 2009, asiga abana batatu aribo Prince, Paris na Bigi. Kuva icyo gihe, umutungo we wakomeje gucungwa n’abawushinzwe, uninjiza amafaranga menshi aturutse mu bikorwa bitandukanye birimo umuziki, uburenganzira ku bihangano bye n’andi masezerano y’ubucuruzi.

Ubu impaka ziri mu rukiko zishingiye ku gihe amafaranga agenewe abana ba Michael Jackson bagomba kuyahabwa, uburyo umurage ucungwa n'uburenganzira bw'abazungura ku migabane yabo.

Icyemezo cy’urukiko gitegerejwe ku wa 4 Ukuboza kikazagaragaza niba ubusabe bwa Paris buzemerwa, niba kizagena n'andi mafaranga bakwiriye guhabwa cyangwa niba kizasaba ko habanza gukemuka ibibazo by’amategeko bikigaragara.

Yagize ati: “Dukeneye ibyo kunywa, urajya ku isoko ugasanga ni Fanta ugasanga ibindi bintu, ariko ugashaka umutobe w’ibitoki byacu ugashaka urwagwa rw’ibitoki byacu ukarubura - byujuje ubuziranenge, ariko ukibaza uti ‘Biraza gukorwa na nde?’”

Yasabye ko Leta yareba uburyo yashora imari mu ruganda runini rutunganya umusaruro w’ibitoki, rwafasha kuwugurira abahinzi no kuwutunganya mu gihe inganda zisanzwe zidashobora kuwugura.

Yatanze urugero rw’uruganda rwa OBIVAR rwahoze rukora, avuga ko hashobora kubakwa cyangwa kongera gushyigikirwa uruganda rw’ubushobozi buhagije, ku buryo mu gihe havutse ikibazo cy’isoko, abahinzi babona aho berekeza umusaruro wabo.

Minisitiri w’Inganda n’Ubucuruzi, Marie-Antoine Kajangwe, yasobanuriye abadepite impamvu inganda zimwe na zimwe zenga inzoga zafunzwe, avuga ko igenzura ryagaragaje ibibazo mu buryo zakoragamo.

Yavuze ko abashinzwe kugenzura ubuziranenge bagiye bagira intege nke, kuko hari igihe barebaga inyubako z’inganda n’ibikoresho zifite, ariko ntibakurikirane niba ibyo bikoresho byakoreshwaga mu buryo bukwiye mu gukora ibicuruzwa byujuje ubuziranenge.

Yagize ati: “Abashinzwe ubuziranenge baragendaga bakarebera uruganda imbere, bakabona rusa neza, runafite ibikoresho bakigendera, bagaruka bagasanga bya bikoresho beretswe ntibyigeze bikoreshwa kandi nyamara uruganda rwo rusohora ibicuruzwa.”

Yakomeje avuga ko hari inganda zagaragazaga ko zifite ibikoresho n’ibindi bisabwa kugira ngo zikore ibicuruzwa byujuje ubuziranenge, ariko nyuma zikajya kubikorera ahandi hatujuje ibisabwa.

Minisitiri Kajangwe yijeje abadepite ko MINICOM n’izindi nzego bireba bari gukora ku mabwiriza agenga uburyo inzoga zikomoka ku musaruro w’ubuhinzi w’Abanyarwanda zigomba kwengwamo, kugira ngo umusaruro ubone isoko kandi abashoramari bashobore gusubukura ibikorwa byabo mu buryo bwubahiriza ubuziranenge.

Yashimye kandi igitekerezo cyo gushora imari mu ruganda runini rushobora gutunganya umusaruro w’ibitoki, kugira ngo rufashe abahinzi kubona isoko mu bihe inganda zisanzwe zidashobora kuwugura.

Yavuze ko icyo gitekerezo kizigwaho, agaragaza ko gishobora kugira akamaro mu gukemura ibibazo by’isoko ry’umusaruro w’ubuhinzi.

Nubwo bimeze bityo, abadepite bagaragaje ko hakenewe igisubizo cyihutirwa, kugira ngo ibitoki bikomeza kwera bitangirika, abahinzi n’abashoramari badakomeza guhomba, kandi ubuziranenge bw’ibinyobwa bukomeze kubahirizwa.

MN202611_66ttfq9xes.t:
Ibi byagarutsweho ubwo abadepite babazaga Minisitiri w’Inganda n’Ubucuruzi, Marie-Antoine Kajangwe, impamvu inganda zafunzwe nyuma y’uko ba nyirazo bashoye imari, bagafata inguzanyo mu mabanki, n’abahinzi na bo bakaba barahinze urutoki bizeye ko bazabona isoko ry’umusaruro wabo.

Depite Christine Mukabunani yavuze ko MINICOM yari ikwiye gukumira ibibazo byagejeje izo nganda ku ifungwa, binyuze mu bugenzuzi bwagombaga kugaragaza ibitagenda neza hakiri kare.

Yagize ati “MINICOM ifite inzego zikora ubugenzuzi. Ndashaka kumva uko byagenze kugira ngo babone ko ziriya nganda zidakora abantu baramaze kwitegura, barashoyemo, ari ku ruhande rw’abanyenganda bari bariteguye bafite imyenda mu mabanki, mbese biteguye ari ho business yabo ishingiye, hanyuma bugacya mu gitondo ngo uruganda rurafunzwe, kandi haragiye hakorwa ubugenzuzi butandukanye.”

Mukabunani yavuze ko n’abahinzi bashishikarijwe guhinga urutoki kuko hari inganda zari zemewe gutunganya umusaruro warwo, bityo na bo bakaba barashoye amafaranga bizeye ko bazabona isoko.

Yagaragaje ko hari abahinzi bageze aho gutekereza ko imitungo yabo ishobora gutezwa cyamunara n’amabanki kubera imyenda bafashe, mu gihe batagishobora kubona isoko ry’ibitoki byabo.

Yabajije MINICOM impamvu itakoze inshingano zayo uko bikwiye, ku buryo ibibazo byari mu nganda byari gukemurwa bitarateza igihombo gikomeye ku bashoramari no ku bahinzi.

Depite Mukabunani yanagarutse ku mabwiriza agenga isuku n’ubuziranenge bw’inzoga za gakondo, avuga ko no mu nzego z’ibanze hakiri urujijo ku bipimo byakoreshwa mu kumenya niba inzoga zengwa n’abaturage zujuje ubuziranenge.

Yagize ati: “Na bo iyo muganiriye barakubwira bati ‘Natwe ntabwo tuzi icyo twashingiraho twemeza ko uriya muntu yakoze ibintu byujuje ubuziranenge cyangwa bitujuje ubuziranenge.’”

Yavuze ko kuba nta buryo bwumvikana bwo gupima ubuziranenge bw’inzoga za gakondo bishobora guteza amakimbirane hagati y’abaturage n’abayobozi, cyane cyane iyo inzoga z’umuturage zimennwe mu gihe atazi neza impamvu zifatwa nk’izitujuje ubuziranenge.

Abadepite basaba ko umusaruro w’ibitoki uhabwa isoko

Depite Erneste Nsangabandi yavuze ko ikibazo cy’ifungwa ry’inganda cyakajije ikibazo cy’isoko ry’ibitoki, kandi ko umusaruro ukomeza kwiyongera mu gihe abahinzi badafite aho bawerekeza.

Yabajije niba, mu gihe MINICOM n’izindi nzego bireba zigitegura amabwiriza y’ubuziranenge, hatashakwa ubundi buryo bwatuma umusaruro w’abaturage ukomeza kubona isoko.

Depite Damien Nyabyenda na we yagaragaje ko uburyo bwo kugenzura ubuziranenge bw’ibiribwa n’ibinyobwa bya gakondo bikoreshwa mu bukwe bwakwigwaho, kugira ngo harebwe niba hari ibyakurikizwa no mu bicuruzwa bigenewe isoko.

Yavuze ko igenzura rikorwa ku rwego rw’umudugudu rishobora gufasha mu gukumira ikorwa n’ikoreshwa ry’inzoga za gakondo zitujuje ubuziranenge, ariko ko hakwiye no kurebwa uko abahinzi b’urutoki batagira uruhare mu ikorwa ry’ibinyobwa bitujuje ubuziranenge barindwa igihombo.

Yasobanuye ko hari abahinzi bateye urutoki bagamije kurubyaza umusaruro ubafasha kwishyurira abana amashuri no kubona ibitunga imiryango yabo, bityo bakaba badakwiye kugirwaho ingaruka z’ibibazo bitagize uruhare mu guteza.

Depite Mazimpaka yagaragaje ubwinshi bw’umusaruro w’ibitoki byengwamo inzoga, ashingiye ku mibare y’Ikigo cy’Igihugu cy’Ibarurishamibare (NISR).

Yavuze ko mu Rwanda buri mwaka haboneka toni 562.968 z’ibitoki byengwamo inzoga, asobanura ko uwo musaruro ukomoka ku buso bunini bw’ubutaka bwateweho urutoki, ku buryo kuwubura isoko bishobora kugira ingaruka zikomeye ku bahinzi.

Yagaragaje impungenge ko ikibazo cy’isoko gishobora gukomeza gukomera, kuko abahinzi badashobora kurandura urutoki bari barateye biteze ko ruzabinjiriza amafaranga.

MN202611_kfhppt851r.t:
Yabivuze ubwo Minisitiri wa MINICIM, Antoine-Marie Kajangwe, yari yitabye abadepite kuri uyu wa Kabiri, ngo abasobanurire ibibazo bagejejweho n’abaturage bijyanye no gutunganya umusaruro w’ubuhinzi no kuwubonera isoko.

Mujawabega yagize ati “Umworozi aratanga litiro y’amata ku mafaranga 400, ariko ubungubu turimo kuyigura twebwe ku mafaranga arenze ibihumbi bibiri, sinzi niba rero kino kibazo kidakwiye gushyirwamo imbararaga zihuse kugira ngo umworozi ahabwe agaciro, ndetse n’Umunyarwanda abone amata, cyane cyane ko kino gihugu kizwi nk’igihugu cy’amata n’ubuki.”

Ati “Numva hari igikwiye gukorwa kugira ngo umworozi ahabwe agaciro n’Umunyarwanda ndetse n’umuturarwanda abone amata.”

Minisitiri Kajangwe yasobanuriye abadepite ko MINICOM n’abafatanyabikorwa bayo bafashe ingamba ko Leta iva mu byo kugena ibiciro by’umusaruro bigakorwa n’abahinzi n’aborozi ubwabo, bakaba ari bo bicara bakabigenza bakurikije ibyo baba bashoye, ndetse n’uko isoko rihagaze.

Yavuze ko kugeza ubu, ku bihingwa bimwe na bimwe nk’ibirayi, umuceri, kawa n’ibindi byatangiye gushyirwa mu bikorwa, kandi bakaba bashaka no kubikora ku mata. Bityo ngo bakaba bumva bizaba igisubizo ku biciro by’amata kuko “usanga yagurishwaga ku giciro kimwe mu gihe cy’umwaka wose.”

Ati “Ariko ubungugu, hazajya habaho inama zibishinzwe (Boards), ku buryo niba ari iy’amata izajya yicara mu gihe cy’imvura hari amata menshi bakagena igiciro bayagurishaho, byagera no mu gihe cy’impeshyi, igihe amata aba yabuze bakongera bakicara bakagena igiciro kijyanye n’icyo gihe.”

Ni ibiganiro bibaye mu gihe, kuba mu Gicurasi uyu mwaka amata yabaye ingume, ku buryo abaturage bageze n’aho bifuza ko yabahenda, ariko akaboneka. Byageze n’aho ku maguriro amwe n’amwe bagena umubare w’udusashi ntarengwa tw’amata bashobora guha umukiliya.

Nko muri Simba, amakuru dukesha umwe mu bahahirayo, avuga ko bo batigeze bazamura ibiciro by’amata ngo bayatange ku biciro by’umurengera nk’uko ahandi hamwe na hamwe bimeze, ariko ko ntawe bashobora kurengereza udupaki (udusashi) dutatu tw’amata.

MN202611_ykh7onjf7p.t:
Ibi babigarutseho mu biganiro y’abadepite bagize Komisiyo y’Imiyoborere n’Uburinganire yagiranye na MINALOC, kuri uyu wa Kabiri, bigamije kureba aho Politiki y’Igihugu yo Kwegereza Abaturage Ubuyobozi n’Ubushobozi yo mu 2021 igeze ishyirwa mu bikorwa.

Depite Sylivie Muyango Mukayiranga yavuze ko kuba serivisi nyinshi zigikorerwa ku rwego rw’igihugu bidahuye n’intego yo gushyira umuturage ku isonga no kumwegereza ubuyobozi.

Yagize ati “Ko duhora tubivuga, slogan yacu nk’igihugu ari ugushyira umuturage ku isonga, none 56% bya serivisi ziracyari ku rwego rw’igihugu. Mu yandi magambo, umuturage ntaraba ku isonga uko tubyifuza.”

Yasabye MINALOC kugaragaza ingengabihe igaragaza serivisi zizajya zimanurwa zikegerezwa abaturage, n’igihe bizakorerwa, kugira ngo ishyirwa mu bikorwa ry’iyo politiki rigaragare mu bikorwa bifatika.

Minisitiri w’Ubutegetsi bw’Igihugu, Dominique Habimana, yavuze ko kuba 44% bya serivisi ari byo bitangirwa mu nzego z’ibanze bitavuze ko izindi zose zigomba kuvanwa ku rwego rw’igihugu, kuko hari izikwiye gutangirirwa ku rwego rwo hejuru.

Yagize ati “Ntabwo bisobanura ko hari ikibazo kubera ko n’ubundi hari serivisi zishobora gutangwa ku rwego rw’igihugu. Ibyo ntacyo bitwaye, icy’ingenzi ni uko tumenya ngo serivisi zirimo gutangirwa ku rwego runaka, ni ho zigomba kuba zitangirwa, kugira ngo izigomba gutangirwa ku rwego rw’ibanze zimanuka zigatangirwa mu nzego z’ibanze.”

Abadepite banagaragaje ko kwegereza abaturage serivisi bidakwiye kugarukira ku kuzishyira hafi yabo gusa, ahubwo ko hakenewe kunoza uburyo bakirwa n’uburyo ibibazo byabo bikurikiranwa.

Depite Muyango yasabye ko amahugurwa ahabwa abayobozi n’abakozi bo mu nzego z’ibanze yakongerwamo ajyanye no kubaha umuturage, bityo abayobozi bakamenya ko guhabwa serivisi nziza ari uburenganzira bw’umuturage, atari ukumugirira impuhwe (kumuha faveurs).

Yavuze ko umuturage agomba guhabwa ibisobanuro ku kibazo agejeje ku buyobozi, ndetse n’igihe bidashoboye gukemuka, akamenyeshwa impamvu n’imbogamizi zabayeho aho gusigara mu gihirahiro.

Abayobozi bahora mu nama aho guha abaturage serivisi

Ikindi kibazo cyagarutsweho ni igihe abayobozi bo mu nzego z’ibanze bamara mu nama, bikaba bishobora gutuma abaturage bajya gusaba serivisi ku biro bakabasanga badahari.

Imibare yatanzwe muri ibyo biganiro igaragaza ko mu minsi 365 igize umwaka, abayobozi bo mu nzego z’ibanze bamara iminsi 65 mu nama. Abadepite basabye ko harebwa uburyo izo nama zategurwa hadahungabanyijwe inshingano zo guha abaturage serivisi.

Depite Muyango yagaragaje ko bidakwiye ko umuturage ajya ku kagari cyangwa ku murenge gusaba serivisi agasanga abayobozi badahari kubera inama za hato na hato.

Abadepite basabye MINALOC gufata ingamba zifatika zo kunoza imitangire ya serivisi, gukurikirana ibibazo by’abaturage no kubasobanurira ibyemezo bibareba, kugira ngo politiki yo kwegereza abaturage ubuyobozi n’ubushobozi igire uruhare rugaragara mu buzima bwabo bwa buri munsi.

Urwego rw’Igihugu rw'Ubugenzacyaha (RIB), rwerekanye itsinda ry'abantu bafatiwe mu byaha bitandukanye birimo kwiba no kwangiza ibikorwa remezo by'amashanyarazi, birimo intsinga.

Aberekanywe ni abantu 11 bakora nk'itsinda bafatiwe mu Turere dutandukanye twiganjemo utwo mu Mujyi wa Kigali n'utwo mu nkengero zawo, bakaba bashobora kugirana isano no kuba ba nyirabayazana w'ibura rya hato na hato ry'amashanyarazi ryagiye rigaragara mu bice bitandukanye by'Igihugu mu minsi ishize.

Abakurikiranwe barimo abanyamahanga babiri bafite ubwenegihugu bwa Uganda, ari na bo baguraga intsinga z'amashanyarazi bakazigurisha mu bihugu by'amahanga.

Bafashwe ku bufatanye bwa Polisi na RIB, bafatanwa intsinga zingana na toni 1.5, zifite agaciro k'arenga miliyoni 20 Frw, zibwe mu Turere dutandukanye turimo utwo mu Mujyi wa Kigali, Kamonyi na Bugesera.

RIB ivuga ko bakurikiranyweho ibyaha bitatu birimo kurema umutwe w'abagizi ba nabi, ubujura no kwangiza ibikorwa remezo, bakaba bafungiye kuri sitasiyo ya polisi ya Kicukiro na Nyarugenge, dosiye yaba ikaba yaramaze gushikirizwa ubugenzacyaha.

Umuvugizi wa RIB, Thierry B. Murangira, avuga ko abafashwe bose bahuriye ku gikorwa cyo gusenya no kwangiza ibikorwa remezo byiganjemo kwiba intsinga z'amashanyarazi.

Ati "Intsinga z'amashanyarazi zibwa mu buryo butandukanye, zibwa n'abantu. Abanyarwanda bakaziba, bakagira aho bazigezaza, naho bakagira uko bazifata bakazambutsa mu bihugu by'abaturanyi. Ni intsinga z'amashanyarazi zo mu bwoko bwa kopa (copper), zibwe mu bice bitandukanye by'Igihugu cyacu."

RIB ivuga ko nyuma yo kumva ibirego bitandukanye by'abaturage yakoze iperereza igasanga ubujura burimo gukorwa atari ubusanzwe, kuko bitari bisanzwe ko intsinga z'amashanyarazi zibwa ngo zijyanwe ku isoko ry'imbere mu gihugu ngo zizagurwe.

Intsinga zafashwe zose, zafatiwe mu rugo rw'umwe mu banyamahanga bafashwe, kuko bose batuye mu Mujyi wa Kigali, ari naho bazikuraga bajya kuzigurisha hanze y'u Rwanda.

Ibyaha bakurikiranweho bihanwa n'amategeko y'u Rwanda, kuko icyo gushyiraho umutwe w'ubugizi bwa nabi no kuwujyamo gihanishwa igifungo kiri hagati y'imyaka 7-10, kigahanwa n'ingingo ya 224 y'itegeko riteganya ibyaha n'ibihano.

Itegeko riteganya kandi ko icyaha cyo kwangiza ibikorwa remezo cyangwa ibikoresho bitanga amashanyarazi, gihanwa n'ingingo ya 51, iteganya igifungo cy'imyaka iri hagati y'imyaka 3-5, ikanateganya ihazabu y'amafaranga y'u Rwanda miliyoni imwe kugera kuri eshanu.

Ikindi ni icyaha cy'ubujura, gihanwa n'ingingo ya 166 y'itegeko, gihanishwa igifungo kiri hagati y'umwaka 1-2, n'ihazabu y'amafaranga y'u Rwanda ya miliyoni 1 kugera kuri 2

Umwanditsi akaba n’umuhanzi w'Umunyarwanda, Gaël Faye yatanze ikiganiro muri Kaminuza ya Georgetown i Washington D.C., muri Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, aho yaganiriye ku gitabo cye 'Jacaranda', cyibanda ku kwibuka amateka no kongera kubaka ubuzima n’umuryango Nyarwanda nyuma ya Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi mu 1994.

Ni igikorwa cyabaye mu rugendo akomeje gukorera muri Leta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika mu rwego rwo kumurikira iki gitabo cye ‘Jacaranda’, aho azasura imijyi itandukanye, akazahurira n’abakunzi b’ubuvanganzo n’abanyeshuri.

Muri iki kiganiro, Gaël Faye yagarutse ku rugendo u Rwanda rwakoze mu kwimakaza amahoro, ubumwe n’ubwiyunge nyuma ya Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi, agaragaza ko kwibuka amateka ari ingenzi mu kubaka ejo hazaza.

Yanasabye ko hakomeza kwitabwa ku kibazo cy’ingengabitekerezo ya Jenoside n’abahakana cyangwa bagapfobya Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi, agaragaza ko ari imbogamizi ikeneye ko abantu bakomeza kuyirwanya.

Igitabo Jacaranda kigaruka ku ngaruka za Jenoside ku bantu n’imiryango, ku kwibuka, ibikomere by’amateka n’uburyo abantu bashobora kongera kubaka ubuzima nyuma y’ibyabaye.

Iki kiganiro cyabereye muri Georgetown University cyatanze umwanya wo kuganira ku ruhare rw’ubuvanganzo mu kubika amateka, kuyasobanukirwa no gufasha ibisekuru bizaza kumenya ibyabaye mu Rwanda.

Igitabo ‘Jacaranda’ cyasohotse bwa mbere mu Gifaransa mu 2024, nyuma kigahindurwa mu Cyongereza na Sarah Ardizzone, kikagera ku isoko ku wa 25 Kanama 2026, kikaba kivuga inkuru y’umwana witwa Milan, wari utuye i Versailles mu Bufaransa mu gihe cya Jenoside yakorewe Abatutsi mu 1994.

Nk’uko bigaragara muri gahunda yashyizwe ahagaragara, uru rugendo rwo kumurika igitabo 'Jacaranda' rukazakomereza mu bindi bigo no mu bindi bikorwa by’ubuvanganzo.

Kuri uyu wa 3 Ugushyingo, aritabira ikiganiro muri Politics & Prose i Washington D.C., ku wa 4 Ugushyingo akomereze muri Villa Albertine i New York, naho ku wa 5 Ugushyingo ajye muri La Maison Française muri Columbia University.

Ku wa 6 Ugushyingo, azaba ari muri Carter Center mu Mujyi wa Atlanta, akomereze muri SCADshow ku wa 7 Ugushyingo mu gihe azakomereza muri Spelman College ku wa 8 Ugushyingo, mbere yo gusoza uru rugendo ku wa 10 Ugushyingo muri Charleston Literary Festival.
